atlantic_bay_scallop.note: A small scallop of the US East Coast bays, from Cape Cod to North Carolina, dredged from late autumn through winter.

crab.note: Species differ by coast: most temperate crabs are fullest from late spring to autumn, Pacific and Mediterranean ones in the cool months.

crayfish.note: Freshwater crayfish are best in the warm months: spring in Louisiana and China, high summer at the Nordic crayfish feasts.

herring.note: Herring is fattest from early summer into autumn, from the first new-season Dutch herring to the autumn Baltic catches.

lobster.note: Cold-water lobsters are landed in quantity from early summer to late autumn, earlier in Newfoundland; tropical spiny lobsters are caught most of the year.

mackerel.note: Atlantic mackerel is oiliest from summer into autumn; Mediterranean shoals come inshore in spring and Japanese saba is prized in autumn and winter.

muskrat_meat.note: Trapped in late winter when the pelts are prime; muskrat suppers are a Lenten tradition around Chesapeake Bay and in Michigan.

mussel.note: Atlantic mussels are plumpest in the cool months after summer spawning; Mediterranean mussels are traditionally eaten in summer.

norway_lobster.note: Langoustines are landed most of the year but are most plentiful and best from spring through summer.

oyster.note: Oysters are firmest in the cold months after spawning, the old rule of months with an R; near the equator mangrove oysters are gathered all year.

sardine.note: Sardines are fattest and best for grilling in high summer and early autumn, when the shoals feed close to shore.

scallop.note: Wild scallops are plumpest from autumn through winter, with full roe before they spawn in spring.

venison.note: Wild deer are traditionally hunted and eaten in autumn and early winter, well fed after summer grazing.
